examples.hint: A hot Jupiter: a gas giant a bit larger than Jupiter that circles its star every 3.5 days. The classic transiting planet.
Flagged by TESS as a possible planet, but it turned out to be two stars eclipsing each other.
An old pulsating star that swells and shrinks every 15 hours, changing its brightness a lot. No planet involved.
A TESS planet candidate with a dip every 3.1 days that nobody has confirmed yet.
Our pipeline measures 4.52 d, NASA's catalog says 9.05 d. When both eclipses look alike, brightness data alone can't tell these apart. Known limitation.

examples.type: Tricky case (transit hidden by star's variability)
examples.hint: A possible planet whose small dips are buried under the star's own brightness changes.
